pages.title: The class of 3/30/20
pages.full_content:
Hello everyone. I have thought about the adjustments that we need to make in order to optimize your learning experience in this class. I've been reading PAD's, and in general, here are my takeaways:

  1. We need to continue to connect live and have intellectual discourse. Reading and doing homework is not motivating.
  2. Small groups work better than larger groups.
  3. I am giving too much work as separate projects. I need to give one weekly assignment only, and one ongoing assignment.
  4. I need to see your faces in real time. I need to look for the confusion on people's faces, and you have been one of my best classes. I genuinely like you guys and I think I personally need the contact for my own sanity.

Many of the questions are related to how pass/fail works. I absolutely need feedback on each class so I can adjust. So I will make the following adjustments:

  1. Class PAD's will be a form to fill out at the end of class. I am going to do away with the participation rubric.
  2. You will have a personal log and one reading due on Saturday. For the reading, I will ask you to answer a question based upon the reading. I will ask you to share the reading response with the class, but the personal log will be private.
  3. We will have three stations, and I'll keep the cohorts you created. The names are too good not to use.
  4. I am going to use the google forms for all homework. Your readings/homework will be shared on this site with the world, so please be aware and use aliases if you don't want the world to see. That said, only those who are really looking will be able to find them.

I will keep the chat rooms, but with only three stations, and you can meet with your cohort privately to complete the stations, on your own time.

We will have a Zoom discussion on Mondays at 9AM followed by the class stations. I will chat with each cohort separately on Zoom and I'll let you know your scheduled time. You will only be required to be live at the 9AM Zoom and with your cohort as you schedule it.

Other that Zoom, this will be your one stop shop homework/class &c.

Here is your homework. Simply fill this in.

1. PAD of Today's Class (Due 3/30) This will be public.

https://forms.gle/FfpSrx5XmfoPAhUS6

2. READING (DUE SATURDAY) Please read Chapter 7 pgs. 243-263. This will be public.

https://forms.gle/FfpSrx5XmfoPAhUS6

3. Please continue your personal log (weekly submission due 4/4) and post to ecampus.

pages.title: How to talk about taboo topics and how to separate from your identity.
pages.full_content:
Procedure:

Why would you want to separate from your identity? Perhaps in order to create a new identity. Ultimately, the best spies can hide themselves as insiders which allow them to "freeride" to get information. One of the best ways to understand and communicate the identity of someone in another culture is to practice the old school debate team exercise of arguing both sides of an argument.

Wednesday assignment- long reading, also presented as a google form right in this page. This will require you to read the textbook. That assignment is due Friday 10 PM. It is going to be about Chapter 7. Look at your identities. How are these identites being shaped (gender, race, ethnic, organizational) by what is happening? Someone noted that their sports team connections were starting to drift apart. This is a way that you might be experiencing a shift in your organizational identity. I asked you to create an alias and a name for your cohort. In this way, I wanted you to play with different types of personal identities. How is your identity helping you or hindering you in coping with what is going on? I am noticing, for instance, that some people are shining online in their work in a way that they may not have in the classroom where others. Anyway, that's work for Friday.

Saturday assignment- your day-by-day log on what you've observed about the week. This week, I want you to notice play. Notice changes in the way you play, what you observe on the street, and challenge yourself to see if you can incorporate play into the life of your Core 5. Here's a bonus. Learn to play poker and play it with people (if you can).

One of the keys in communicating with other cultures comes in discovering how, even when your venn diagram doesn't intersect the venn diagram of someone else's culture you're still able to communicate that you understand what the other person is saying. One way to do this is to do something called reflective listening this is how it works:

"I'm so proud of myself. I have not watched a second of the hearings nor have I watched the fake news in weeks. Those of you who know me well are aware that this feat is a miracle. I'll be sure to get out to vote TRUMP 2020! Life is great!"

To listen reflectively, you can say, "So what you're saying is that you are not watching the news which is a great accomplishment of self-control for you. You definitely support Trump, and you're feeling that life is great. Am I hearing you right?"

The person confirms. You ask if they have more to explain or if you got it.

The next step is to move to the affect reflection. "That must make you feel so free and confident about your decisions."

Wait for a response. Finally, you can say, "I can understand that if you support Trump all this news could just bring you down and not watching the news would make you feel good. That makes lots of sense."

You have validated the person without necessarily agree with the person to validate their opinion.

Your cohort's task today is to practice validation. One of you will play the role of choosing a controversial opinion. It doesn't matter if you believe the opinion or not. Take some time to think about a reasonable argument to make for the position you choose (going to offer some doozies). The job of the other person is just to reflect and validate the opinion of the other person without necessarily agreeing.

Station #1:

Take a minute or two to think of a one to two minute argument supporting one of these ideas:

  1. The coronavirus is invented by aliens who want to delay us from getting to Mars.
  2. The world is actually flat.
  3. College tuition is too low and should be raised.
  4. People can actually live underwater for an hour if they believe they can.

The job of the talker is to express the idea to the cohort. The job of the listener is to listen actively and reflect what the person is saying back to them, and to validate what they're saying without agreeing or disagreeing or judging.

The rest of the cohort will act as judges to determine if the listener was objective without ceeding agreement. You have a minute, and then you'll switch until everyone has a chance to be the talker and the listener.

Station #2:

Reading.. So, what does this have to do with identity? You need to be strong in your own identity to be able to validate others.

pages.title: Art and Validation 4/6
pages.full_content:
Greetings. Please continue your exercises in validation, starting with the reading and practicing with your cohort.

First, we will get a mini-lecture from yours truly.

Station #1

[googleapps domain="docs" dir="document/d/e/2PACX-1vRh2fd_YcV4hNw94DRuUqkK_l-7DARSVKQ4gGOUcZwdnvQY2BxEy7iKg3XUoZtc7DbhS4lFztQb4A6u/pub" query="embedded=true" width="100%" height="900" /]

Station #2

Graphic arts and music.

We're talking about validation, and understanding how people need affect validation, emotional validation before they can proceed logically. 

Interestingly, music is a way that people experience emotional validation. People can feel “understood” by a particular work of art. In fact, on some level, the function of art is to validate. But response to music is a learned response and driven by culture. My own research looked at music from a neurological point of view (I looked at Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata and The Soviet National Anthem, now also the Russian national anthem). When we respond to music, we respond on a pre-verbal level, and the sounds trigger neurons in our brain to respond with signals to the throat to imitate the sounds, to the body to move and if we are musicians, these responses also happen in the fingers to correspond to the instrument we play.

We can see in what’s happening now in lockdown that art is an engine of culture. It preserves the action/perception loop in a way, evoking certain times in a person’s life, and very recognizably different from culture to culture. It works the way validation works.

Validation is a very effective form of grooming. It creates trust enough for people to believe that the groomer is not a freerider, and therefore, at least for a time, can be treated as someone in a person’s circle. 

Validation through music is very interesting. The listener can feel emotionally validated by, for instance, sad music even though they may not understand the actual words. In some cases, the music can be so validating that the musician can slowly become part of a person’s imagined inner circle, and the fandom the person feels is so deep that the fan forgets that the musician doesn’t know them.

Validation through art might work in the same sort of way. 

This picture of the woman is not a picture of quarantine.. But does it evoke the concept of quarantine for you? Does the artist inadvertently validate something you might be feeling now about your work during quarantine? Please read the professors' responses and add your own on the form.

pages.title: Class Number 1: Wednesday, September 9, 2020.
pages.full_content:
Welcome to your first class.

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (creating a display for the Peace Corps display case in The Great Hall, and sending those very NJ items to children somewhere in the world)
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy and frameworks and how they explain our actions.
  5. Work as a team to create a cultural consulting group that advises an individual on a real-life cultural problem.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

"When we are happy or amused we make our own unique noise and often times can't control it that leads to slapping the term laughter onto the action. You know what I’ve realized?
The fact that we can’t unfeel something. We just get used it. Like suppose we’re sitting on a cold surface, it’s cool at first but then it starts getting warmer. It’s not that the surface suddenly got hotter, it’s just that we got used to the coldness.

Or when someone keeps treating you terrible and after a while, you just don’t acknowledge it anymore cause you’re used to it. And that’s just really heartbreaking. The fact that we get used to something so much that we completely forget it’s there." -Molly A. Sibilia

[youtube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yosEFnhS3TI&w=640&h=360]

Local song. We are also part of the world.

From the readings:

  1. The chapter mentions the phrase “culture is shared”. How can they throw in such a vague statement yet say how each culture is unique in their own ways? Are there ways they are shared? Yes maybe way back into its origins, years and years ago. However, it’s like saying personality is shared but contradicting that and saying, your personality is what makes you unique. What separates a culture but makes it unique at the same time?-BB
  2. After reading this chapter a question that popped into my mind is how does language develop over time. I remember in my history classes looking at historical documents such as thedeclaration of independence and being shocked at how different the language was. Reading these documents was almost like reading another language. I am really interested to know how this happens. I also wonder that in a hundred years from now people will have trouble understanding the language that we use today.
  3. The second question that I was pondering while reading was how do certain cultures come up with their norms. For example in the United States people shake hands when meeting each other. (Prior to CoronaVirus) -KM
  4. Is the effect of dopamine evolutionarily dampening due to the easiness of accessing it? Now if we want to hear our favorite song or watch our favorite movie we can do it almost instantaneously with technology— there is no longer any real reward -HT

Activity #5: Not Funny!

Nas is a guy travelling the world with his fiancee. They visited Albania. Notice in this clip the way he laughs at the uncomfortable moment and discuss who, if anyone is having endorphins released in this exchange.

[youtube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6-DLKR5BYk&start=43&end=187&w=700&h=700]

Moving on... You can opt out of this, but read what you have to do.

Here are some jokes. Read them and discuss with your group if you think they're funny (do they release endorphins for you?). If you feel too uncomfortable to participate in this assignment, you can sit it out. I love my state. The opinions here IN NO WAY reflect the feelings of management. In fact, I chose these particular jokes because I didn't find them funny.

*Alert: Some people will find them funny, and some will find them offensive. They are listed here for the purposes of learning something about grooming communities. Which of these jokes release endorphins, and which triggers alarms (releases the fight or flight hormone cortisol)

  1. "I was forced to go to New Jersey.. I know, my boss hates me.. but thank God, I recently got back home from Louisville to celebrate Christmas. Speaking about thanking God, on the plane, I met a preacher who was also coming home on a flight from Newark Airport. He says he was sent to a parish in NJ. I didn't ask him what he did to deserve that.. But he told me he just has to go back to Kentucky every year to preach his Christmas sermon because it just doesn't work in New Jersey. It could work anywhere else, just not in New Jersey. 'Why?' I asked. 'What's the sermon about?' He said, "It's about the fact that Jesus could have been born anywhere. But I am convinced Jersey is the exception.' "Why?" I asked him. He threw up his hands. "Because where in New Jersey are you going to find a virgin or three wise men?"
  2. "Has anyone been to the East Coast? I had to land in New Jersey once. Yeah, I know. Have pity on me. Anyway, Jersey stinks. I mean it literally. It actually smells bad. I guess it has to smell bad so that blind people can hate it too."
  3. What's the difference between New Jersey and yogurt? Yogurt has an active, living culture.
  4. What happens when a blonde moves from NY to NJ? Both state's IQs go up.
  5. What are the four happiest years of a Jersey boy's / Monmouth student's/ Monmouth athlete's/ MU Comm major's/ life? Third grade. Is there anything you can insert into that blank that makes it the least funny/ the most prickly?

Laughter is ancient. It predates speech in humans, and we share it in common with other apes. Think of the centrifugal/ centripetal forces involved in these jokes. Do they unite the people who find the jokes funny against those who are offended?

So, after all that, we still don't know how language started? Not exactly, but we can speculate...

The Stations:

Activity 1 &2: 8:45-9:05

Activity 3: 9:05-9:15

Activity 4: 9:15-9:25

What is your job today? 2 minutes to assign jobs. Today all groups will be doing the same activities, and I'll be hopping in and checking on each group.

Groups 1-5 all start with activity 1.

Activity #1+2

THIS IS ACTIVITY 1.

I could give you the task of communicating using sounds today, but instead, your job will be to develop a language using facial expressions and hand signs. Voice has more advantages, but it's too easy to "cheat". Your group will try and develop a sign language that no other group can interpret. When we get back together, we will have a contest to see who can communicate the best (in order to get a resource.. extra credit!) other groups can attempt to steal your signs. The rules: You can't use spelling (creating letters). Your language should have a syntax (English syntax is (adjective)Noun, verb, object) but that's not the only syntax. American Sign Language doesn't worry so much about word order. Some languages mark subject, object and verb with sounds that are put at the end (or beginning) of a word to mark if the word is a subject, object or verb. This way, you can put the words in any order you please.

You also need to create a lexicon of five verbs, five nouns and three adjectives at least. And you need three pronouns: I you and other. You can also create plurals, if you choose.

Your MGE .

Activity 1: negotiation

Negotiation Exercise:1.Role playing: You are trying to buy a leather jacket from a street trader in a foreign country whose local currency is valued at 50,000 to 1 of yours. You really like the jacket, which is a good fit, well made and style. But you think the trader is asking too much. Can you negotiate an acceptable price for both of you?Buyer: You have a maximum of 750,000 units of local currency and 100 units of your own. You also have your credit cards. Decide what you want to pay and the tactics you will employ making concessions. A similar jacket in your country will cost about 130 units of your currency.Trader: You have sold seven of these jackets to foreigners in the last few days. The lowest price you received was 300,000 units, the best prices 800,000 units. Most foreigners did not even haggle with you. The jacket cost you 200,000 units. You know that you can buy them more cheaply with foreign currency than your own, which is shaky on the exchange market. In fact, 30 units of the Buyer’s currency would buy you another jacket. You are determined however to make a good profit on this deal.

Activity 2: Your MGE

Your group will do a final project. Each person has a part to play. 

Your grade will be determined based upon the individual work you accomplished, but the more the group cooperates, the more likely you are to succeed.

Each group will have the following members. We used these same designations when I did my walkabouts of NJ, and they work really well for the division of labor.

Poison Ivy: Leader, will fill in jobs that are left undone, makes sure everyone knows what they are doing, and are on point.

Ant: Keeps track of meeting times, fills the sheets that outline who was present at each meeting and who did what for the final project.

Wolf: Makes sure that rules are respected, makes sure that there is no plagiarism, and that conflict is resolved in the group (some barking and some validating is required)

Bat: Is in charge of communication. Makes sure that everyone has each other’s contact information and establishes the best possible way for everyone to communicate.

Otter: Handles technical issues, in charge of editing, recording and film work. 

In charge doesn’t mean exclusive. Each task may require cooperation from various people. But the tasks determine whose academic “head will roll” if things aren’t done. The Poison Ivy’s head almost always rolls, but they aren’t the only one.

As I reflect on the past semester, I have to say that this Intercultural Communication class, this particular collection of students was a silver lining in a crazy, often dark time. 

I admit that teaching you students, getting to know you as well as I could in this remote environment was often the highlight of my day.

So, thank you for getting up early, sharing your insights, letting me know what was going on with you. As long as Wordpress lasts, this class will be archived here, so if you want to leave a message to your future self, or students who will only experience what Covid was remotely, distantly, here’s a chance to leave something paraphrastic, or affective or dialectic on these pages. 

It may not be a huge legacy, but it’s something that some distant day, you may just revisit to amuse yourself. I leave the comment section open, and I ask you to leave a comment, maybe one thing you’ve learned from me, but even more importantly, something you’ve learned or benefitted from in your relationship with the other students in this class. Say something to your fellow classmates. 

There is an old story about an English Professor who, when giving the graduating class a speech, he said “I hope that after four years of study at this institution, you will have learned that it isn’t who you know, but whom you know.”

The point is, long after the main points of what is taught here have been rerouted through your dendrites and the neurons have stopped firing in that way that allows you to know concepts like grooming communities, Dunbar’s number, freeriders, empathy, uncertainty avoidance, cultural frameworks in general, TPAD’s and NSEW critiques, you will maintain some of the human connections you have made here. 


I will continue to hope to meet you in person in the fall, please, please come around. But even if I don’t see a single one of you, I do hope that at least some of you will see each other again,  maybe even for the first time.

pages.full_content:
Government's role in culture:

In the late '90s, when Asia went through a huge financial crisis, South Korea's leaders decided to use music to improve its image and build its cultural influence. So the country's government poured millions of dollars into forming a Ministry of Culture with a specific department devoted to K-pop.

"It turns out that the Korean government treats its K-pop industry the way that the American government treats its automobile and banking industry, meaning that these are industries that have to be protected," Hong says.

This included doing things like building massive, multi-million dollar concert auditoriums, refining hologram technology, and even helping regulate noeraebangs — karaoke bars — to protect the interests of K-pop stars.

"They wanted Korea of the 21st century to be like America of the 20th century where America was just considered so universally cool that anything made in America would automatically be bought."

source

South Korea, with .66% of the world's population, has 5% of the world's pop music revenue. One third of all venture capital in Korea is spent on pop culture. The result has been a multi billion dollar industry.

timer: That's one minute. Let's move on.

WILL WE STAND UP?

Assignment:

(Ten minutes)

During this part of the class, you will have a seven minute lecture or a homework or reading. Today I give you a homework assignment that you can start now. I will include this in your ecampus work. I suggest you read a bit and look over the questions you will be asked (TPAD) that will basically be how you respond to every reading. Talk to the members of your cohort and ask me questions when I come around.

Here is your first reading:

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (creating a display for the Peace Corps display case in The Great Hall, and sending those very NJ items to children somewhere in the world)
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy and frameworks and how they explain our actions.
  5. Work as a team to create a cultural consulting group that advises an individual on a real-life cultural problem.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

What will happen each class?

I understand zoom burnout, and don't want you to suffer. I divide my class into five sections when I teach live, and for ten minutes or so, the cohorts (groups of five) rotate through five tasks. I will be assigning permanent cohorts by class. This means you MUST sign in through monmouth.zoom.us . It is an essential time saver and we will go over how to do that.

Each Monday you will get a short reading that you can probably do in class, but to hand in no later than 4:30 on Tuesday if you want to be graded out of 100 and each Wednesday you will get a longer reading that you will have to turn in by Friday by 4:30 if you want to be graded out of 100. My goal this semester is to attempt to have neither of us work on weekends, and I will be grading your work at 4:30 on Tuesdays and Fridays. Please let me know if the work I assign is too much.

With these reading TPAD's you'll learn. I will drop the lowest three.

I don't give exams, quizzes or tests, but I will be giving two major grading events and a final project. I will review the syllabus in depth on Wednesday and you will get your first assignment (to read Chapter 11 in the textbook). If you don't have the textbook yet, don't worry. The problems and limitations of intercultural communication are small but somewhat concerning depending on how you look upon it. It can always be concerning coming in contact with a new culture because you don't want to offend anyone. Racism, stereotypes, and prejudice were all topics mentioned in the reading piece which can be mistakenly used towards a culture when learning to communicate with them. Mistakes like this can be detrimental towards coming together as one even though they may be unintentional. This is why both sides of the conversation need to be educated on accepting mistakes and learning about the other culture. Can you think of a situation where mistakes like this have led to tragedy, comedy, or unwarranted anger, either in your personal life, or in the world at large? If not, could you imagine such a situation?

What do you think are the sources of the Hikimori culture in Japan? Does the Pandemic now favor those who practiced that culture?

The main problem is the problem of humanity, most people are weak minded, and therefore will result to the easy out, in this case prejudice, racism will create a team mentality and empower those who are to weak to go against the grain, whether it be a soldier being given unlawful orders or a kid being forced into a gang, social constructs are strong and a reality. "When we are happy or amused we make our own unique noise and often times can't control it that leads to slapping the term laughter onto the action. You know what I’ve realized?

pages.full_content:
Our last class on unity.

[googlemaps https://www.google.com/maps/d/embed?mid=1FwpznZKpgTr66BNRuvkSf9FCZF83NIBF&w=640&h=480]

We are united, not just with other humans, but even with other animals, in many interesting ways, including the fact that we have the ability to laugh, sing, recognize names, gestures, and we can tell pretty well, universally, what other humans' emotional reactions mean.

We also know that we have a basic grooming community of no more that about 150 individuals, with a core group of 5. People can come and go from this core group, and the core group could include fewer people, but generally we have five people in our central core.

Take 8 minutes to listen to the lecture.

We know that all humans have the ability to acquire language, even if those languages are different.

So, with all these similarities, why are there different cultures and different languages?

  1. We need to know who has our back.
  2. We need to be special to someone, and we need to hold others special to us.

So now that we have examined the similarities between cultures, we will start to explore the differences that make cultures unique.

We will also begin to talk about techniques to communicate across cultures, after we've acquired a language.

8 minutes:

Break into your groups and discuss the lecture. One spokesperson will have to give a summary, either terms, paraphrastic, affect or Dialectical analysis. Try and tie the lectures to all the lectures that have come before.

10 minutes: Each group has two minutes to discuss the lecture with the group. Try to tie it to all the lectures that have come before.

PART II: Validation-

And we will start that with validation.

This is a great, universal technique. In some form, it has been practiced by cultures across the globe, and we will try it here. It is a way that we can groom, using language.

This is a super-important technique, so I will practice it with you first, and then you can break into your groups and practice it.

pages.full_content:
Tying up loose ends, Part One.

14ymedio’s Faces of 2020: The Independent Artists of Cuba’s San Isidro Movement

14ymedio, Havana, 24 December 2020 – The San Isidro Movement, born just two years ago, has shaken the political situation in Cuba in the last weeks of 2020 by crossing borders and putting the regime in a bind of incalculable dimensions.

At the end of 2018, a group of independent artists who rejected Decree 349 – a law through which the Government sought to regulate the arts sector by making cultural work outside the state orbit de facto impossible – formed this movement in the Havana neighborhood that gave the movement its name.

The collective took center stage with a protest held in November to demand the release of one of its members, Denis Solís, sentenced to eight months in prison for the alleged crime of contempt. Several members of the group began a hunger and thirst strike, which some were able to maintain for more than a week until the headquarters of the Movement, where they were gathered, was raided by the political police, who detained them for several hours.

In solidarity with them, in addition to that they have found outside of Cuba, a group of at least 200 people demonstrated in Havana in an unusual protest that managed to begin a failed dialogue with the cultural authorities. The harassment of the Movement continues, with arrests, acts of repudiation and accusations of terrorism, but they have lit the fuse of a dream to open a new horizon for the opposition in 2021.

Loose ends.

Activity 2: Your MGE

Dossier: A dossier that includes:

  1.  the cultural frameworks that you have observed about the culture, including at least 5 frameworks and a short explanation of what that means to the negotiation.
  2. A description of do’s and don'ts, at least eight, focused on cultural taboos.

You need 2 dossiers. You will be graded individually on one dossier position. 

2 situational papers: You will research the specific situation and understand the point of view of each side, so, not just an “objective” assessment of the situation, but the situation as described by each side. These need to be well-researched and can be bullet points.

You need to include:

  1. An overview of the issue.
  2. Talking points you can make to gain the other side’s interest.
  3. How you anticipate the other side might push back.

There can be a one-paper overlap.

Second part of the project:

A filmed negotiation that either does or doesn’t reach an agreement (5 minutes) You can divide the time among students, or you can have one person in charge of tech, one “editing” the statements to make sure they are accurate, two (or more) on-camera debaters. I want to know what each individual job was.

Tech person

2 debaters

Fact-checker/ detail checker (one side)

Fact-checker/ detail checker  (the other side)

Your group will do a final project. Each person has a part to play. 

Your grade will be determined based upon the individual work you accomplished, but the more the group cooperates, the more likely you are to succeed.

Each group will have the following members. We used these same designations when I did my walkabouts of NJ, and they work really well for the division of labor.

Poison Ivy: Leader, will fill in jobs that are left undone, makes sure everyone knows what they are doing, and are on point.

Ant: Keeps track of meeting times, fills the sheets that outline who was present at each meeting and who did what for the final project.

Wolf: Makes sure that rules are respected, makes sure that there is no plagiarism, and that conflict is resolved in the group (some barking and some validating is required)

Bat: Is in charge of communication. Makes sure that everyone has each other’s contact information and establishes the best possible way for everyone to communicate.

Otter: Handles technical issues, in charge of editing, recording and film work. 

In charge doesn’t mean exclusive. Each task may require cooperation from various people. But the tasks determine whose academic “head will roll” if things aren’t done. The Poison Ivy’s head almost always rolls, but they aren’t the only one.

Here is your default issue. You can take on a different issue, if that's what your group decides, but remember that it has to be international and it has to require a measurable goal on both sides. Here are some possibilities:

Palestinians and Israelis setting parameters for safe May 15 protests.

Doctors without borders negotiate with EU officials to allow passage to a boatload of refugees from Lybia to Sicily.

Cattle ranchers vs. environmentalists or native peoples representatives in the Amazon

Inclusion of Taiwan in World Health Organization COVID coordination (one negotiator takes the side of China, the other of Taiwan)

Debate over shared power between Taliban forces and the government of Afghanistan

Nuclear Arms limitation in Iran (Iran and US negotiators)

Russia's presence in the Crimea.

  1. Choose an issue to work on
  2. Assign jobs and deadlines to accomplish those jobs
  3. Ant: Record who was present at this meeting, and in the last five minutes, ask each member of the cohort what they contributed to the project.
  4. Set up at least one time to meet outside of class time to work on the project, either on the dossier or on working on making the recording of the negotiation "work".

Assignment:

(Ten minutes)

During this part of the class, you will have a seven minute lecture or a homework or reading. Today I give you a homework assignment that you can start now. I will include this in your ecampus work. I suggest you read a bit and look over the questions you will be asked (TPAD) that will basically be how you respond to every reading. Talk to the members of your cohort and ask me questions when I come around.

Here is your first reading:

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/él). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans may or may not have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Activity 2

Activity 3

Talk in your group about what defines your hometown/region.

  1. Are you from the Jersey Shore? If not, where are you from? What are the differences in food and dress? Have you eaten at White Castles? Have you had "real pizza?" What about bagels? Have you gone to a diner? 
  2. What is food like where you have been? What are the differences between here and there? Even in the traditions of each meal, how do they differ? Do families eat late at night? When is the main meal? Do kids drink wine?
  3. How often do you eat with your hands versus with a utensil per week? How often is meat part of your meal? Fish?
  4. Do you eat facing each other, or a screen? How far in advance is a meal planned?
  5. How often is the meal in your home cooked versus purchased?
  6. What are the major eating holidays?

Activity 4:

In the previous round, you did a survey that talked about Geert Hofsteade's cultural dimensions test and you took a survey that compared your own dimensions to that of a specific country. Now, as a group, look at the cultural dimensions we measured. Talk about your own upbringing and your local culture. Read the dimensions and describe where you as an individual, as a member of your family and larger community fit within these dynamics. Often in cultures of immigrants, there is a disconnect between the cultural dynamic in the household and the one "on the street".

High vs. Low Power Distance: Refers to the beliefs regarding the proper distribution of power in a society. It expresses how much less powerful members of a community should accept that power is allocated unequally. How a society deals with social inequality is the main concern in this dimension. People in civilizations with high power distance accept hierarchical structures where everyone has a place, and no further reasoning is necessary to justify that hierarchy. In comparison, societies with low levels of power distance work to equalize power distribution and demand tangible reasons for power inequalities in the government of their countries. Do older siblings get privileges that younger ones don't? Do bosses get privileges that workers don't?

Individualism vs. Collectivism: Indicates how the interests of the individual are weighed against the interest of the community. A loosely-knit social structure in which people are expected to look out for and check in primarily with themselves denotes a high level of individualism. By contrast, cultures with low levels of individualism are attuned toward the group and typically feature a closely-knit social structure in which people look to their relatives, countrymen, coworkers, and other members of their communities when determining what course of action they will take. Does the good of the many outweigh the good of the one? Should you go as far as your abilities will allow? Should it be "from each, according to his ability, to each according to his need?"

Masculinity vs. Femininity: Cultures high in masculinity tend to revolve around success, competition, and rewards. By contrast, cultures low in masculinity concentrate on values like nurture, modesty, and empathy. High-masculinity cultures often produce more assertive and decisive leaders, whereas low-masculinity cultures tend to produce more agreeable, inclusive, and compassionate leaders. Is this a problematic way to see masculinity and femininity?

High vs. Low Uncertainty Avoidance: Measures how comfortable a culture is with ambiguity and uncertainty. High uncertainty avoidance cultures uphold strict moral and behavioral standards and tend to frown on unconventional behavior and ideas. They want the future taken care of and planned for according to what has been proven to work in the past. By contrast, low uncertainty avoidance cultures are more tolerant of unusual ways of doing things and are not as disapproving of ambiguity.

Long vs. Short-term Orientation: Measures whether a culture aims for long-term goals on the basis of how the world is projected to change or prefers to achieve short-term goals using how things have been up till now as a guide. Cultures with a long-term orientation are future-focused and promote thrift and investments that take a long time to come to fruition. In contrast, cultures with short-term orientation uphold long-standing traditions as a way of ensuring stability and tempering the speed of social change. I put a syllabus together with a timetable, but that has changed, and it may not be clear to people. What does that indicate about the culture of this class? How could that cause culture shock?

Indulgence vs. Restraint: Measures the degree to which cultures attempt to regulate their impulses toward gratification. Cultures high in indulgence encourage pleasure and enjoyment as innate human desires associated with taking pleasure in life and having fun, whereas cultures with a restraint orientation frown on the satisfaction of desires and attempt to control enjoyment through social rules and taboos. Where do your people fit in? Are you an athlete? Do you think this standard is different among athletes?

Activity 1

You are doing three things. You are selling something, trying to convince people of something (or to do something) or organizing a party for people. Discuss with your group.

Central question: Pretend you are entering a culture with high power distance. How would you make a request of a boss? If you were in a social situation, what would you be watching for? You might have to refer back to last time's definitions, but try to see if you can remember first. How do you organize a party when there is a great deal of power distance?

Pretend you are trying to promote an idea or sell something to a person who is a member of an individualistic society. How would you do that? On the other hand, how would you promote an idea or sell something in a collectivistic society? What sort of activities are best for individualistic societies? Which for collectivist societies?

In the same way, what would be your pitch if the society was more "Masculine" or "Feminine" (I still hate that term)

Long and Short Term orientation?

Activity 2

After what happened last time, I asked you to bring something to listen to this section individually. I did bring some old headphones. Please re-listen to this lecture. Ant, tell your group when to begin, so we can finish together.

[soundcloud url="https://api.soundcloud.com/tracks/885775747" params="color=#ff5500&auto_play=false&hide_related=false&show_comments=true&show_user=true&show_reposts=false&show_teaser=true&visual=true" width="100%" height="300" iframe="true" /]
profe frank · ICC1

Activity 3

With me. Let me know if you won the Quizlet on Monday.

Activity 4

Three things you can't guess about me. Write three things down on a piece of paper that people may have never guessed about you, and put them in the can. Discuss why you thought that thing would surprise your cohort.

Activity 5

Bat- make sure each person can speak for around a minute and fifteen seconds. It can be a dialog, but we must hear from all the voices in the group.

Each group member takes one of the cultural dimensions, and thinks about an example from their own lives that might show an extreme of each of these, or you can discuss this collectively. You all decide.

High vs. Low Power Distance

example: Did you ever meet someone famous? How was that different than interaction with someone not famous?

Individualism vs. Collectivism

Were you ever in a highly competitive situation when it was every person for themselves? Were you ever in a situation where people seemed to put other people down or talk themselves up?

Were you ever in a situation that you didn't think you were being recognized for who you were, but only for how well you fit in?

Masculinity vs. Femininity

Have there been times that you felt you could do things on your own but people just wanted to hold your hand, maybe too much?

Have there been times when you felt you were given a task that you were expected to do without any guidance or support? (Maybe like your first TPAD?)

High vs. Low Uncertainty Avoidance

Do you have friends or acquaintances that encourage you to try risky things, or new experiences?

Have there been situations in your life where you have run into people who are afraid to step outside the box?

Long vs. Short-term Orientation

Would you consider yourself a "spender" or a "saver"? If you own a vehicle, do you practice regular maintenance, or tend to fix things when they go wrong only? Where would you say your family culture lies within this dimension?

Indulgence vs. Restraint

Who spoils you? Where do you turn for discipline? If you played sports, did everyone get a trophy in the end? Do you think American culture is more indulgent or restrained? How do other parts of the country compare to US?

pages.full_content:
Jersey Shore Artifact Project: In the next two weeks, you will be asked to come up with an artifact that reflects something about the New Jersey shore. For those of you who are from out of town, it is a good opportunity to learn about this environment, and to interact with you cohort. You will choose an item, something inexpensive and able to be mailed in a care package somewhere in the world. The more New Jersey shore specific, the better. You will then create an index-card sized description (so we can exhibit these items in a display case) and make a short video (two minutes) describing the artifact and its importance to the culture of the Jersey shore. The project is due February 28.

Quizlet with link

Freewriting warm-up : 5 minutes

Start with objects like a candle, a bell, a wine bottle, a trophy, a loaf of bread, a suit of clothes or a dress, a game, a book, something in a frame. Think about the object and speak for it.

Here are some examples. "I am a green candle. Every Sunday, during football season, I was lit to bring luck to the Eagles. Because I am part of a Jewish and Catholic household, and the traditions related to lighting candles were important to both religions, we candles maintained a sort of spiritual power and could help the Eagles win football games, unfortunately, our mojo was not quite strong enough." or, "I hang in the closet zipped in a plastic bag, to keep me fresh. So far, I was only ever worn once, but it was very special. The girl who wore me wore me on her quinceañera: There was a mass, then a big party..." Or, "I am a trophy. I was given to a kid during a little league picnic. I sit on a shelf collecting dust, partly because everyone who played on the team got a trophy, so it wasn't really for anything special.[

  1. Think about your transitional object. What was it for you? For me it was a teddy bear. It was named Domenico, after my grandfather who died before I was born. It is still somewhere in my closet, sixty plus years old. My son is also named Domenico, not after the bear, but after my grandfather. When I was little, my mom was afraid that I would choke on the eyes, so she cut them off and sewed on green felt. For one of my daughters it was a special blanket that she named "Speshie". Do you have a transitional object? Discuss with your group
  2. Share your freewriting with your cohort.
  3. Look at my response to your TPAD. Please grade yourself in the appropriate box.
  4. Lecture- Please remember that this lecture is based upon Robin Dunbar's work, and he is very controversial. This is a way of explaining things, but may not be the only way.}

profe frank · EDUCATION- ANCHOR OF CULTURE
  1. Individualism vs. Collectivism:
    • Did you attend schools where teamwork and group projects were emphasized, or were you primarily assessed based on individual performance?
    • How did your educational experience encourage or discourage independence and self-reliance?
    • In what ways did your educational background value or prioritize community involvement and collaboration?
  2. Power Distance:
    • How hierarchical was the structure of your educational institutions? Were teachers and students expected to interact as equals, or was there a clear distinction in authority?
    • Were students encouraged to question authority figures such as teachers and administrators?
    • Did your educational environment promote open dialogue and discussion, or were there implicit rules about who could speak and when?
  3. Uncertainty Avoidance:
    • How did your educational system handle ambiguity and uncertainty in learning materials and assignments?
    • Were students encouraged to explore different perspectives and approaches to problem-solving, or was there a more rigid, standardized curriculum?
    • How did your educational background prepare you to deal with change and adapt to new situations?
  4. Long-term Orientation vs. Short-term Orientation:
    • Did your educational system emphasize long-term goals and planning for the future, or was there more focus on immediate outcomes and results?
    • How did your educational experience shape your attitudes towards persistence and perseverance in achieving your goals?
    • Were there cultural or societal expectations regarding the importance of education for future success in your community?
  5. Masculinity vs. Femininity:
    • How were gender roles and expectations addressed in your educational environment?
    • Were there subjects or activities that were considered more appropriate or suitable for one gender over the other?
    • Did your educational background encourage the development of traditionally masculine traits such as assertiveness and competitiveness, or were more emphasis placed on nurturing and cooperation?

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/él). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you have a good technique for negotiating, and you understand that the real purpose of (intercultural) negotiating is to establish a relationship from which you can build solutions, not necessarily for coming up with solutions immediately.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

Why is this critical, especially in this class?

Because if you can't get along with your own cohort, that may be from a similar cultural background, what possible chance do you have to get along with people who have vastly different backgrounds?

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Learn how to negotiate across culture
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy (cultural dimensions) and frameworks and how they explain our actions.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

What will happen each class?

We will have a walk on song, a short lecture and rotate through stations that reinforce the work we do in our class.

Please understand that I myself am part of an older tradition that emphasized student input, discovery and error as part of a process. Students who are used to looking for clear expectations, who feel that they can stay ahead of the curve by doing assignments written into a calendar, and basically checking boxes, might feel discouraged by this class. If you want to go ahead, explore other areas of inquiry, do other readings, use this class to answer questions I haven't asked, just let me know and we can work out a way for this to happen, as long as your avenues of inquiry pull the class along with you.

What this means is that you will not see a class that shows slides, assigns readings, tells you what is on a test and then you study, learn what the test entails, and then do some presentations or papers that further illustrate the points made.

We live in exciting times, and I am excited to see what use you make of new tools emerging. I am hoping that in short order, you will be able to take over the class and teach me something. If all you get out of the class is a good grade, then you may have passed the class, but the class has failed you.

pages.title: #0: About this class
pages.full_content:
Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/él). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans may or may not have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (creating a display for the Peace Corps display case in The Great Hall, and sending those very NJ items to children somewhere in the world)
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy and frameworks and how they explain our actions.
  5. Work as a team to create a cultural consulting group that advises an individual on a real-life cultural problem.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

What will happen each class?

I divide my class into five sections when I teach live, and for ten minutes or so, the cohorts (groups of five) rotate through five tasks.

Each Monday you will get a short reading that you can probably do in class, but to hand in no later than 4:30 on Tuesday if you want to be graded out of 100 and each Wednesday you will get a longer reading that you will have to turn in by Friday by 4:30 if you want to be graded out of 100. My goal this semester is to attempt to have neither of us work on weekends, and I will be grading your work at 4:30 on Tuesdays and Fridays. Please let me know if the work I assign is too much.

With these reading TPAD's you'll learn. I will drop the lowest one.

I don't give exams, quizzes or tests, except for those oral ones, but I will be giving two major grading events and a final project.

By the way, if you are reading this, email me and tell me you've read it and I'll give you extra credit if you are among the first six to email me.

Homework/reading activity- attempting to keep weekends homework-free.

  1. Individualism vs. Collectivism:
    • Did you attend schools where teamwork and group projects were emphasized, or were you primarily assessed based on individual performance?
    • How did your educational experience encourage or discourage independence and self-reliance?
    • In what ways did your educational background value or prioritize community involvement and collaboration?
  2. Power Distance:
    • How hierarchical was the structure of your educational institutions? Were teachers and students expected to interact as equals, or was there a clear distinction in authority?
    • Were students encouraged to question authority figures such as teachers and administrators?
    • Did your educational environment promote open dialogue and discussion, or were there implicit rules about who could speak and when?
  3. Uncertainty Avoidance:
    • How did your educational system handle ambiguity and uncertainty in learning materials and assignments?
    • Were students encouraged to explore different perspectives and approaches to problem-solving, or was there a more rigid, standardized curriculum?
    • How did your educational background prepare you to deal with change and adapt to new situations?
  4. Long-term Orientation vs. Short-term Orientation:
    • Did your educational system emphasize long-term goals and planning for the future, or was there more focus on immediate outcomes and results?
    • How did your educational experience shape your attitudes towards persistence and perseverance in achieving your goals?
    • Were there cultural or societal expectations regarding the importance of education for future success in your community?
  5. Masculinity vs. Femininity:
    • How were gender roles and expectations addressed in your educational environment?
    • Were there subjects or activities that were considered more appropriate or suitable for one gender over the other?
    • Did your educational background encourage the development of traditionally masculine traits such as assertiveness and competitiveness, or were more emphasis placed on nurturing and cooperation?

TERMS

Intercultural Communication

The exchange of information between individuals from different backgrounds of learned behavior.

Culture

A series of behaviors that are invented, not acquired, and passed on through learning within a group.

Verbal Communication

The exchange of information through spoken or written language.

Nonverbal Communication

The exchange of information through non-linguistic means, such as body language, facial expressions, or gestures.

Sender

The individual or entity that initiates a message in the communication process.

Receiver

The individual or entity that interprets and processes the message in the communication process.

Miscommunication

A failure to convey information accurately or understand a message as intended, often due to cultural differences or other factors.

Cultural Context

The background, habits, and perceptions shared by members of a culture that influence how messages are sent and interpreted.

Filtering

The process of separating relevant information (meaning) from irrelevant information (noise) in communication.

Sojourner

An individual who temporarily resides in a different culture and must adapt to its communication norms and practices.

Noise

Anything that interferes with the transmission or understanding of a message. It could be literal background noise, but in this context, it more broadly includes any irrelevant information or distractions that could impede clear communication. Culture teaches us what is noise and what isn't.

You will go in a circle, with the previous listener becoming the speaker, and the person to the speaker's left becoming the listener, until everyone has gone.

Start with your bat.

The speaker asks the listener if they have time to hear what they have to say.

The listener takes a second to clear their own mind, take a breath with the listener, and, hopefully say , "yes". The speaker thanks the listener for their willingness to hear what they have to say.

The speaker shares a particular frustration they experienced during the week. It can be anything, trivial or big. The person to the left of the person who expressed the frustration will mirror back what the first person has said. The listener should not offer a solution or add information. Merely paraphrase what the person has said. Do not try to fix the problem. Do not say "Me too!". Just mirror.

If you are the listener, and the person has gone on too long to remember everything, ask the person to stop. "Please. I want to make sure I'm hearing everything you're saying... you said that... and then mirror back. Then the person can say "please continue... The speaker should take note of how they feel after having been mirrored.

The speaker then becomes the listener, and the person to the speaker's left around the circle becomes the listener. While the speaker and the listener are sharing, the others should try to be mirroring, in their heads, what the speaker is conveying.

This is the actual letter that President Leahy wrote to the faculty after we demonstrated at the Great Hall following a union meeting. The task is to validate the President's position, whatever your personal opinion on the matter might be.

Please come up with a validation.

  1. Reflect what the President has said. Have someone take notes, and someone read. Pause in the validation, and go only so far in the reading where the validator remembers what was said without having to read it, and then reflect it back.
